rows.title: Trade court strikes down a second round of Trump tariffs
rows.standfirst: The Court of International Trade has struck down a second round of global tariffs ordered by President Trump, after his earlier import taxes were outlawed by the U.S. Supreme Court.

rows.title: She helps families in need. As gas and grocery prices rise, she needs help, too
rows.standfirst: She has spent decades helping others struggling to make ends meet. Now the rising cost of gas and groceries has left Dalene Basden feeling the strain herself.

rows.title: Gas prices keep rising, but do big oil companies plan to drill more? Not so far
rows.standfirst: The war in Iran has pushed global oil prices higher, which boosts oil company revenues. But major U.S. oil companies aren't signaling plans to increase production to bring down prices at the pump.

rows.title: Campaign staffers tell NPR they make 'thousands' betting on their own candidates
rows.standfirst: Campaign staffers are turning private polling data into personal paydays. They describe the election prediction market as a "Wild West" for staffers.

rows.title: Trump crypto, Trump ballroom and Trump drones
rows.standfirst: What do a Florida-based drone company, a crypto billionaire, and a European steelmaker have in common? Ties to President Trump. Since returning to office, the president, as well as his family and friends, have inked a number of business deals that raise questions about conflicts of interest. On today’s show, we scrutinize three of these deals.

rows.title: The man who changed TV news
rows.standfirst: When the U.S. and Israel bomb Iran and start a war, we know about it moments after it’s started — sometimes even moments before. When Russian tanks cross the border into Ukraine, we watch as it’s happening. This access to immediacy — our ability to be there as history is unfolding — much of that is possible, thanks to the vision of CNN founder Ted Turner.

rows.title: 'A trailblazer, a rabble-rouser, a do-gooder': CNN founder Ted Turner dies at 87
rows.standfirst: Turner had a larger-than-life personality, and used it to launch the country's first 24/7 all-news network.

rows.title: Have you lost or are worried about losing SNAP benefits? NPR wants to hear your story
rows.standfirst: NPR wants to hear from people impacted by changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

rows.title: A trip to Europe? In this economy? Expensive flights keep vacations closer to home
rows.standfirst: Travel advisers are seeing Americans picking cheaper domestic travel destinations over Europe.

rows.title: How we got free agents in baseball
rows.standfirst: Curt Flood was the best center fielder in baseball and one of the game’s highest paid players. He took the St. Louis Cardinals to the World Series three times. Then he got traded to the Phillies. He didn’t want to go. But baseball’s rules said he had no say in the decision. He could either go to Philly or quit the sport. Instead, Flood took Major League Baseball to court.

rows.title: When will the Iran war hit food prices?
rows.standfirst: The US-Israel war in Iran is already being felt by American consumers at the gas pump, but when — and how badly — could it be felt at the supermarket?

rows.title: How much is the war hitting American's bottom line?
rows.standfirst: There already was an affordability crisis in the U.S. How the war with Iran is making life more expensive.

rows.title: NPR went looking for Polymarket's Panama headquarters. It's elusive
rows.standfirst: The hugely popular prediction market was shut down by U.S. regulators in 2022 and re-opened in Panama, where it has benefited from tax and legal benefits for years.

rows.title: The Iran war sent jet fuel prices sky-high. Here's what air travelers should know
rows.standfirst: Fuel is airlines' second-largest expense, and getting even costlier due to the U.S. war with Iran. Airlines are looking for ways to cope, starting by hiking checked baggage fees for most fliers.

rows.title: If you are struggling to make ends meet, NPR wants to hear from you
rows.standfirst: With gas prices and other necessities at record highs, families are struggling with costs. NPR wants to know how you're coping.

rows.title: How AI is speeding new business creation, especially among Gen Z entrepreneurs
rows.standfirst: Entrepreneurs are turning to AI to speed the creation of new businesses, with Gen Z leading the way. That's according to a new report from the payroll software firm Gusto.

rows.title: Jury orders Boeing to pay $49.5 million to family of 737 MAX crash victim
rows.standfirst: A federal jury in Chicago awarded $49.5 million to the family of Samya Stumo, a young woman who was killed in the second of two Boeing 737 MAX crashes within months of each other in 2018 and 2019.

rows.title: The MAHA movement is coming to school cafeterias. Here's what that means for kids
rows.standfirst: U.S. school districts worry it could get even more expensive to prepare a meal under new federal dietary guidelines, as they also contend with cuts to programs that helped them buy local food.

rows.title: How Trump's central bank beef could hurt the economy
rows.standfirst: A new documentary from Frontline PBS, called “The President vs. the Fed”, helps us make sense of the unprecedented power struggle between the world’s most powerful politician and the world’s most powerful bank. You can watch the film, directed by Frontline Correspondent James Jacoby, on Frontline’s website, YouTube channel, or the PBS app.

rows.title: The secret meeting that launched OPEC
rows.standfirst: Recently, a listener wrote in with a question about OPEC and oil prices. She was prepping for a camping trip… thinking about how much it costs to fill up her diesel-guzzling camper van at the pump.

rows.title: Foreign ticket holders from World Cup teams' countries won't have to pay bonds to enter U.S.
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration is suspending a requirement that visitors from countries that have qualified for the World Cup and bought tickets for the tournament pay as much as $15,000 in bonds to enter the U.S.

rows.title: Senate confirms Kevin Warsh as next chair of the Federal Reserve
rows.standfirst: Warsh has argued there's room for the central bank to lower interest rates, but that could be challenging at a time of rising inflation.

rows.title: Short flights are popular. Will they last?
rows.standfirst: Some flights are less than 100 miles, and they're the backbone of the U.S. air system, linking small towns and big cities. But short routes were in decline even before jet fuel costs spiked.

rows.title: Should NATO be pay-to-protect?
rows.standfirst: NATO was formed after World War 2 as a collective security alliance that would prevent future world wars. But President Trump sees NATO more like a transaction between countries where allies have to pay up or be left undefended. On today’s episode: How NATO is actually funded, why this longstanding alliance is under strain, and how the U.S. could pay the cost for these frayed relationships.

rows.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman takes the stand to fend off Elon Musk's accusations he 'stole a charity'
rows.standfirst: The trial pits two of tech's most famous personalities against each other and could lead to seismic changes for the maker of ChatGPT.

rows.title: Transportation Secretary Duffy filmed a reality show, funded by firms he regulates
rows.standfirst: Secretary Duffy, his wife and nine kids took a "Great American Road Trip" to celebrate America's 250th. They say no taxpayers funded the project. But a nonprofit with transport-related sponsors did.

rows.title: Inflation jumps to its highest level since 2023. Here are 3 things costing a lot more
rows.standfirst: Rising gasoline prices pushed inflation to its highest level in almost three years in April. Consumer prices were up 3.8% from a year ago.

rows.title: The economic chilling effect of Trump's immigration crackdown
rows.standfirst: New research finds that ICE raids and deportation fears disrupted local economies, reduced work among undocumented immigrants, and may have hurt some U.S.-born workers too.

rows.title: The clipping economy: How short-form video 'clippers' are overrunning the internet
rows.standfirst: Short-form clips of long interviews and shows are taking over the internet. But behind the sea of social media clips are marketplaces offering freelance clippers money per view.

rows.title: Prediction markets are threatening national security. Who's gonna fix it?
rows.standfirst: It’s the Wild West of online betting. Prediction markets have been plagued by insider trading allegations, ethical questions and even national security concerns. Today on the show, what are sites like Polymarket doing to self-police, and what other regulations might be necessary? We talk to one U.S. senator with some ideas.

rows.title: A trillion dollar question: Will SpaceX's Starship launch go well?
rows.standfirst: Ahead of a much anticipated IPO, SpaceX is carrying out a critical test of its giant, stainless steel rocket. Investors will be watching closely.

rows.title: Walmart plans price cuts using tariff refunds as shoppers get skittish
rows.standfirst: Now that the U.S. government must refund most tariffs, Walmart says it might put its refund money toward lowering store prices. Executives say the cost of gas has shoppers increasingly under stress.

rows.title: Spencer Pratt is 'winning the internet,' but can he become mayor of Los Angeles?
rows.standfirst: Pratt, a former reality TV star, is flooding social media with edgy humor, AI slop and combative rhetoric as a way of grabbing attention and winning the vote of the very online. It's a strategy some political experts see as the future of online campaigning.

rows.title: So ... how long until these oil prices get REALLY bad?
rows.standfirst: The US-Israel War in Iran is almost three months in and oil prices have risen, but they’re not catastrophic … yet. Why isn't the price of oil even higher? We learn about how the world is adapting to the blocked Strait of Hormuz.

rows.title: Elon Musk's SpaceX IPO plans reveal blockbuster spending on rockets and AI
rows.standfirst: The company is on track to pull off the largest IPO in history — making CEO Elon Musk even wealthier.

rows.title: Meta slashes 8,000 jobs as it pivots towards AI
rows.standfirst: Facebook and Instagram's parent company has been investing huge sums of money in AI, but it lags behind competitors.

rows.title: After the Kars4Kids ad is banned in California, we check in on nostalgic jingles past
rows.standfirst: A California judge has given Kars4Kids 30 days to either take its ads off the air or update them to disclose its affiliations to a Jewish charity based in the Northeast.

rows.title: Bipartisan home affordability bill passes the House
rows.standfirst: The bill is meant to encourage home construction, and would ban corporate investors from buying up more homes to rent out.

rows.title: It's come to this: Human certification in the age of AI slop
rows.standfirst: In an era of AI slop, we find out how some artists are seeking out human verification for their work. Plus, we prove our own episode is 100% human-made.

rows.title: Vacation and why Americans take so little
rows.standfirst: Do you work more for more money? Or work less for more time? For some, this is the ultimate economic choice.

rows.title: U.S. government to drop tax claims against Trump in broadening of IRS settlement
rows.standfirst: As part of the settlement agreement, the U.S. is "forever barred and precluded" from examining or prosecuting President Trump, his sons and the Trump organization's current tax issues, according to a document posted to the DOJ website.

rows.title: Minnesota becomes first state to ban prediction markets
rows.standfirst: While dozens of states have taken legal action against the controversial industry, Minnesota is the first state to pass a law making it a felony for companies like Kalshi and Polymarket to operate.

rows.title: The missing men of the American marriage market
rows.standfirst: A new study suggests the growing educational and economic divide between men and women is reshaping marriage and family life in America — leaving many women with a shrinking pool of economically stable partners.

rows.title: Why GLP-1s aren't lowering employers' costs
rows.standfirst: The vast majority of employer health plans do not cover GLP-1s for weight loss. But roughly 20% do, many believing it will help their bottom line. Perhaps when employees take Wegovy or Zepbound, they’ll need less medical care tied to health issues from obesity. Today on the show, can GLP-1s save employers money in the long run?

rows.title: Why you should care about 2 power companies merging. Hint: affordability
rows.standfirst: NextEra Energy plans to acquire Dominion Energy to create the largest electricity producer in the United States.

rows.title: United Airlines flight to Spain pulls U-turn, apparently over Bluetooth device name
rows.standfirst: The flight to Palma de Mallorca diverted back to Newark late on Saturday. Air traffic audio and social media posts indicate an onboard Bluetooth device raised security concerns.

rows.title: The sneaky way companies get new chemicals into our food
rows.standfirst: 99% of chemicals in our food right now were added without FDA approval. Many were added in secret, through a sneaky loophole built into the 1958 Food Additives Amendment.

rows.title: Here's how we're coping with high gas prices, according to Costco and Walmart
rows.standfirst: Sky-high gas prices have drivers going out of their way for discounts at the pump. Oil executives warn that even higher prices might be on the horizon.

rows.title: The D-List pop star purgatory
rows.standfirst: We love a pop princess, but what about the pop peasants?

rows.title: Obsession, the most fun job in China, and a new green card policy
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!). It’s our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: FIFA's World Cup ticket sales outraged fans. Now they are under investigation
rows.standfirst: FIFA has always had a peculiar way to sell tickets to the World Cup. It never faced any major issues — until prices soared for the 2026 tournament.

rows.title: Saudi’s LIV Golf exit is just the start
rows.standfirst: Is Saudi Arabia no longer a golf state? The Saudi sovereign wealth fund poured billions into culture and sports in the last decade, none more high profile than LIV Golf, a rival to the PGA. So why is it reversing course now?

rows.title: This is how close American households are to the financial edge
rows.standfirst: A new report shows that nearly half of U.S. households did not earn enough to cover their necessities in 2024.

rows.title: These swing voters are adding high gas prices into their political calculations
rows.standfirst: As part of NPR's Swing Shift project checking in with swing voters, these Americans are split on who is to blame for high gas prices but they all agree it has an impact on their personal finances.

rows.title: Trump wants a gas tax holiday. There's a much bigger problem looming
rows.standfirst: Suspending the federal gasoline tax could save drivers up to 18.4 cents per gallon. But it would drain the fund meant to cover roadbuilding and repairs — a fund that's already in trouble.

rows.title: DOJ charges Google staffer over Polymarket trades netting $1.2 million
rows.standfirst: It's the second known case of the federal government filing criminal charges against someone who allegedly used insider information to make a large profit on a prediction market site.

rows.title: NPR's newsroom shrinks through buyouts and layoffs
rows.standfirst: At least 18 NPR journalists have accepted buyouts and another 10 have been laid off as the public media network attempts to save money and reorganize the newsroom.

rows.title: More people are going hungry now than at the height of the pandemic
rows.standfirst: Food insecurity affects more families now than during the coronavirus pandemic, according to a new survey from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

rows.title: The leaked tapes that show how the rich avoid taxes
rows.standfirst: Tax avoidance -- that is, legally reducing your tax bill -- is as American as apple pie. But the line between tax avoidance and tax evasion is often a grey one.

rows.title: What the movies teach us about recessions, memestocks and gold
